summary: Adds versioning to WebDAV with new HTTP methods, headers and resource types, so tools can track revisions of web resources. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: WebDAV lets a program edit files on a web server. RFC 3253 adds the missing half: a record of every saved state. Each saved state gets its own permanent web address, so a link to "the version from March" keeps working, and two people can edit different copies and merge them later.

questions: what does the checkout method do in webdav
subtitle: How WebDAV remembers every saved state of a web resource, with check-out, check-in, labels, merges and baselines.

tldr.problem: WebDAV lets clients edit resources on a web server, but there was no standard way to keep the history of those resources, name past states, or let several people work in parallel.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds new methods such as VERSION-CONTROL, CHECKOUT, CHECKIN, LABEL and MERGE, along with headers, properties and reports. A resource under version control gets a version history, and each saved state becomes an immutable version with its own URL.
tldr.outcome: A server can support any combination of features, from simple linear versioning to workspaces, baselines and activities. Basic servers are advised to implement one of three packages so that clients stay simple.

today: RFC 3253 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2002, and no later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it. It builds on the WebDAV extensions in RFC 2518 and on HTTP/1.1 in RFC 2616.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document specifies a set of methods, headers and properties that define the WebDAV versioning extensions to the HTTP/1.1 protocol. Versioning is concerned with tracking and accessing the history of important states of a web resource, such as a standalone web page.

The benefits of versioning in the context of the worldwide web include the following. A resource has an explicit history and a persistent identity across the various states it has had during the course of that history, which allows browsing through past and alternative versions of a resource; the modification and authorship history of a resource is frequently critical information in itself. Resource states, that is, versions, are given stable names that can support externally stored links for annotation and link server support, because both annotation and link servers frequently need to store stable references to portions of resources that are not under their direct control.

WebDAV Versioning defines both basic and advanced versioning functionality. Basic versioning allows users to put a resource under version control, determine whether a resource is under version control, determine whether a resource update will automatically be captured as a new version, and create and access distinct versions of a resource. Advanced versioning provides additional functionality for parallel development and configuration management of sets of web resources. An implementer interested only in basic versioning can skip the advanced sections.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things make versioning worth having: every saved state gets its own address that never changes, and the history records who changed what and when.

sections.title: Terms
sections.content:
Version control is a set of constraints on how a resource can be updated. A resource under version control is either checked-in or checked-out, and the version control constraints apply only while the resource is in the checked-in state. A versionable resource is a resource that can be put under version control. When a versionable resource is put under version control it becomes a version-controlled resource, which can be checked out to allow modification of its content or dead properties by standard HTTP and WebDAV methods.

A version resource, or simply a version, is a resource that contains a copy of a particular state of a version-controlled resource. A version is created by checking in a checked-out resource, and the server allocates a distinct new URL for each new version, which will never be used to identify any resource other than that version. The content and dead properties of a version never change. A version history resource contains all the versions of a particular version-controlled resource, and a version name is a string chosen by the server to distinguish one version of a version history from the others.

When a version-controlled resource is checked out and then checked in, the version that was checked out becomes a predecessor of the version created by the checkin. A client can specify multiple predecessors for a new version if the new version is logically a merge of them. A root version is the version in a version history that is an ancestor of every other version in that history. When a second successor is added to a version this creates a fork, and when a version is created with multiple predecessors this creates a merge. A server may restrict the version history to be linear, but an interoperable client should be prepared to deal with both forks and merges.

A workspace is a collection that contains at most one version-controlled resource for a given version history. A working resource is a checked-out resource created by the server at a server-defined URL when a version rather than a version-controlled resource is checked out, and unlike a checked-out version-controlled resource it is deleted when it is checked in. A label is a name that can be used to select a version from a version history, and it can be assigned by either a client or the server.
sections.plainLanguage: The vocabulary matters because each term is a distinct kind of thing on the server. A version is frozen forever, the version-controlled resource is the live editable one, and the version history is the collection that holds the frozen ones.

sections.title: Basic Versioning Packages
sections.content:
A server may support any combination of versioning features. However, in order to minimize the complexity of a WebDAV basic versioning client, a server should support one of three packages. The core-versioning package is version control alone. The basic-server-workspace package is version control, workspace, version history and checkout. The basic-client-workspace package is version control, working resource, update and label.

The core-versioning package supports linear versioning by both versioning-aware and versioning-unaware clients, and a versioning-aware client can use reports and properties to access previous versions of a version-controlled resource.

The basic workspace packages support parallel development of version-controlled resources. Each client has its own configuration of the shared version-controlled resources and can make changes without disturbing another client's. In the basic-server-workspace package all persistent state is maintained on the server, and each client has its own workspace resource allocated there, which identifies a configuration of the shared resources. The server workspace package is appropriate for clients with no local persistent state, or for clients that wish to expose their working configurations to other clients.

In the basic-client-workspace package each client maintains in local persistent storage the state for its own configuration. When it is ready to make its changes visible, it allocates a set of working resources on the server, updates them, and then uses the set to update the version-controlled resources. Using working resources instead of updating the version-controlled resources directly lets sets of consistent updates be prepared in parallel by multiple clients. A server that supports both basic workspace packages will interoperate with all basic versioning clients.
sections.plainLanguage: Rather than one giant feature set, the RFC offers three bundles. A server picks one, and a client then knows roughly what to expect.

sections.title: Creating a Version-Controlled Resource
sections.content:
In order to track the history of the content and dead properties of a versionable resource, a user can put the resource under version control with a VERSION-CONTROL request. Such a request performs three distinct operations. It creates a new version history resource; in basic versioning that resource is not assigned a URL and is not visible in the URL space, though when the version history feature is supported each version history resource is assigned a new distinct and unique server-defined URL. It creates a new version resource and adds it to the new version history resource, with the body and dead properties of the new version resource a copy of those of the versionable resource, and the server assigning it a new distinct and unique URL. And it converts the versionable resource into a version-controlled resource, which continues to be identified by the same URL, and gains a DAV:checked-in property whose value contains the URL of the new version resource.

A versionable resource and a version-controlled resource are not new types of resource and introduce no new resource type. They are any type of resource that supports the methods and live properties defined for them, in addition to all the methods and live properties implied by their own resource type. A collection, for example, is a versionable resource if it supports the VERSION-CONTROL method.

So before the request there is one, non-version-controlled resource, and after it there are three separate, distinct resources: the version-controlled resource, the version resource and the version history resource. Because the version-controlled resource and the version resource are separate resources, a method applied to a version-controlled resource is applied only to that resource and not to the version resource currently named by its DAV:checked-in property.
sections.plainLanguage: Putting a file under version control creates two extra things on the server: the history that holds all the states, and the first frozen copy. The original file stays where it was and gains a pointer to that copy.

sections.title: The LABEL Method
sections.content:
A LABEL request can be applied to a version to modify the labels that select that version. The case of a label name must be preserved when it is stored and retrieved, and when comparing two label names to decide whether they match a server should use a case-sensitive URL-escaped UTF-8 encoded comparison. If a LABEL request is applied to a checked-in version-controlled resource, the operation must be applied to its DAV:checked-in version.

The request body must be a DAV:label element containing at most one DAV:add, DAV:set or DAV:remove element, each of which holds a label name. The request may include a Label header and may include a Depth header; if no Depth header is included, Depth:0 is assumed and standard depth semantics apply. The response to a successful request must include a Cache-Control header of no-cache.

The preconditions require that a version-controlled resource be checked in, that a label named in a Label header select a version in the version history, and that a label added with DAV:add not already appear in the label set of any version in that history. The postconditions require that a label added or set must appear in the label set of the specified version and must not appear in the label set of any other version in the history, and that a removed label must not appear in the label set of any version in the history.

Separately, for methods such as GET and PROPFIND, a label can be given in a Label request header so that the method is applied to the version selected by that label. The value of a label header is the name of a label encoded using URL-escaped UTF-8, so the label "release B.3" is sent as Label: release%20B.3. A Label header must have no effect on a request whose URL does not identify a version-controlled resource.
sections.plainLanguage: A label is a nickname for a version, such as "release B.3". Anyone can then fetch or inspect that version by name without knowing its internal URL, and the RFC insists a label names exactly one version in the history.

sections.title: The MERGE Method
sections.content:
The MERGE method performs the logical merge of a specified version, the merge source, into a specified version-controlled resource, the merge target. If the merge source is neither an ancestor nor a descendant of the checked-in or checked-out version of the merge target, the MERGE checks out the merge target if it is not already checked out and adds the URL of the merge source to the DAV:merge-set of the merge target. It is then the client's responsibility to update the content and dead properties of the checked-out merge target so that it reflects the logical merge.

The client indicates that it has completed the update by deleting the merge source URL from the merge set and adding it to the predecessor set. As an error check for a client forgetting to complete a merge, the server must fail an attempt to check in a version-controlled resource with a non-empty merge set.

When a server is able to update the merge target automatically it may do so unless DAV:no-auto-merge is specified. To notify the client that a source was merged automatically, the request must add the URL to the DAV:auto-merge-set property rather than the merge set, and the client then deletes it from that set and adds it to the predecessor set.

Multiple merge sources can be specified in one request. If DAV:source identifies a version, that version is a merge source. If it identifies a version-controlled resource, its checked-in version is a merge source. If it identifies a collection, the checked-in version of each version-controlled resource that is a member of that collection is a merge source. The request URL identifies the set of possible merge targets. The response for a successful request must be a 207 Multi-Status identifying all resources that the request modified, and must include a Location header with the URL for the new version created by the checkin.
sections.plainLanguage: Merging says: take this other branch of the history and fold it into mine. The server marks the merge as pending, the client does the actual folding, and the server refuses to let the client check in until it says the folding is done.

sections.title: Advanced Versioning Features
sections.content:
The advanced features add the machinery for parallel development and for managing sets of resources as a configuration. A workspace is a collection holding at most one version-controlled resource for a given version history, so each user can have their own set of checked-out copies without interfering with anyone else. The working-resource feature lets a client create its own editable copy on the server, update it, and then apply it to the shared version-controlled resource, which is how several users prepare consistent changes at the same time.

The label feature adds the named selection of versions described earlier. The baseline feature adds the concept of a baseline, a named set of resources and their versions that can be compared against another baseline, together with the BASELINE-CONTROL method that creates one. The activity feature adds activities, with the MKACTIVITY method, so that a group of related checkouts can be tracked and reported on together. The version-controlled-collection feature covers collections whose membership itself changes over time, so that the set of versions that make up a collection is itself versioned.
sections.plainLanguage: The advanced part is about working on many files together: a workspace for your own edits, a baseline as a named snapshot of a whole configuration, and an activity as a group of related checkouts.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All of the security considerations of WebDAV discussed in RFC 2518 also apply to WebDAV versioning. Some aspects of the versioning protocol help address security risks introduced by WebDAV, but other aspects can increase these risks.

On auditing and traceability, WebDAV increases the ease with which a remote client can modify resources on a web site, and so increases the risk of important information being overwritten and lost, whether through user error or malice. Versioning helps by guaranteeing that previous information is saved as immutable versions and is therefore easily available for retrieval or restoration. The version history also provides a log of when changes were made and by whom, and when requests are appropriately authenticated the history mechanism provides a clear audit trail.

On access control, versioning provides a variety of links between related pieces of information, which can increase the risk that an authentication or authorization error allows a client to locate sensitive information. If version history is not appropriately protected by access control, a client can use the history of a public resource to identify later versions that the user intended to keep private. A versioning client should be designed to handle a mixture of 200 and 403 responses, because a user may be authorized to access the content of a version-controlled resource but not its checked-in, checked-out or version-history properties.

On obscurity, version URLs, version history URLs and working resource URLs are generated by the server and can be obfuscated so as not to draw attention to them, for example a version of a salary page might be given an opaque numeric URL. On denial of service, the auto-versioning mechanism can result in a large number of resources being created on the server, since each update could create a new version, which increases the risk of an attack that exhausts the storage capability of a server. This risk is especially significant because it can be an unintentional result of something like an aggressive auto-save feature in an editing client. A server can reduce the risk by using delta storage techniques, by limiting auto-versioning to a locking client, and thereby decreasing the number of inadvertent version creations.
sections.plainLanguage: Versioning helps with recovery and with keeping an audit trail, but it also creates more doors into the same data, and an auto-saving editor can quietly fill a server with copies.

messages.label: VERSION-CONTROL /foo.html
messages.note: Puts a versionable resource under version control.

messages.label: 200 OK
messages.note: A version history and a first version have been created, and the resource now has a checked-in property.

viz.caption: THE STATUS CODES THE VERSIONING METHODS USE

items.label: OK
items.desc: The request succeeded. VERSION-CONTROL answers with this when a resource is put under version control.

items.label: CREATED
items.desc: A new resource was created as a result of the request.

items.label: MULTI-STATUS
items.desc: The request was applied to several resources and the body lists the result for each.

items.label: FORBIDDEN
items.desc: A precondition failed and repeating the request would always fail.

items.label: CONFLICT
items.desc: A precondition failed but the user might resolve the conflict and try again.

items.label: LOCKED
items.desc: The resource is write-locked and the request did not carry the right lock token.
